newsitem.title: USA: U.S. warship, Marines head for Sierra Leone.
newsitem.headline: U.S. warship, Marines head for Sierra Leone.

text.p: The U.S. Navy helicopter ship Kearsarge is steaming toward Sierra Leone with 1,200 Marines but the military has received no request to evacuate Americans from the West African nation, the Pentagon said on Tuesday.
U.S. Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said the situation in Sierra Leone was calm after a weekend military coup that ousted the elected government.
But he said the Kearsarge would be offshore within 24 to 48 hours from its previous station off Zaire and would be "ready to conduct contingency operations if necessary."
The United States on Monday called for restoration of the civilian government in Sierra Leone, joining the United Nations, the Organisation of African Unity and South Africa in condemning the coup.

The new army rulers have said in Sierra Leone, where there are about 400 Americans in the capital of Freetown, that they have opened land borders and air and seaports. But a dusk to dawn curfew remained in force.

Bacon told reporters that the Kearsarge left Atlantic waters off Zaire, where it had been on stand-by for a possible evacuation from the capital of Kinshasa, on Saturday night and would stop off Sierra Leone en route to its regular station in the Mediterranean.

"It is planning to stop probably 20 or so miles (32 km) off the shore and wait and see what happens," he said in response to questions. "There has been a (State Department) request for us to be available if necessary, but no request to be more than available."
Bacon said there were thousands of other foreigners in Sierra Leone, including United Nations' workers, but that the Pentagon had received no requests so far for any evacuations.
"Our hope is that the situation will remain calm in Freetown and that the threat to Americans or any other foreigners will go away and that democratically-elected government will return," he said.
The State Department on Monday condemned the coup and called on the military to return power promptly to elected leaders and Parliament.
State Department spokesman John Dinger told reporters on Tuesday that some 38 Americans worked at the U.S. Embassy in Freetown but there was no plan at the moment to evacuate them.

Dinger said there had been no shooting in the capital on Tuesday, although a rocket-propelled grenade had earlier struck the embassy. But the spokesman said the United States did not believe that the embassy had been deliberately targeted.
